title: Banking Services
summary: A bank is an institution that accepts deposits of money from the public, repayable on demand or otherwise, and lends money to those who need it. Unlike a moneylender, a bank is regulated by the RBI, deals with the public at large, gives loans on proper security at interest rates governed by the RBI, follows a flexible and lawful recovery process and accepts deposits; a moneylender lends from his own funds, often against gold or land, at very high interest decided by himself and recovers strictly. Banks provide funds for business and play a vital role in a nation's development: they mobilise savings, give finance to trade, industry and agriculture, create credit, make payments easy and help balanced regional growth.

Central bank — the Reserve Bank of India (established 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934; nationalised in 1949; head office Mumbai). It issues currency, is the banker to the government and the bankers' bank, controls credit and interest rates, and manages foreign exchange; it does not deal with the public. Commercial banks — public sector (majority shares held by government — SBI, Bank of Baroda), private sector (majority held by private individuals — ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank) and foreign banks. Cooperative banks — primary credit societies, central and state cooperative banks, urban cooperative banks. Development and specialised banks — EXIM Bank (finances and guides export and import), SIDBI (Small Industries Development Bank of India), NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development).

Primary functions: (1) accepting deposits — savings, current, fixed and recurring; (2) granting loans and advances — loans for a fixed period against security; cash credit (borrow up to a limit against stock or security); overdraft (current account holders may withdraw more than their balance up to a limit); discounting of bills of exchange. Secondary functions — agency functions: collecting cheques, bills, dividends and interest; making payments such as insurance premium and rent; buying and selling securities; acting as trustee or executor. General utility functions: issuing demand drafts and traveller's cheques; safe-deposit lockers and safe custody of valuables (the relation is then bailor and bailee); letters of credit; foreign exchange; supplying trade information (not an advance).

Savings bank account — for people with limited income who want to save for future needs; any amount can be deposited at any time, withdrawals limited in number, moderate interest. Current deposit account — for businessmen, companies, schools, hospitals; any number of deposits and withdrawals, the most liquid; no or little interest; overdraft facility. Fixed deposit account — a lump sum deposited for a fixed period at a higher interest rate, not withdrawable before maturity without penalty (e.g. saving ₹2,00,000 to gift a son on graduation). Recurring deposit account — a fixed amount deposited every month for a fixed period (e.g. ₹5,000 a month); interest higher than savings. Multiple option (flexi) deposit — a savings account in which balances above a set limit move automatically to a fixed deposit, earning more interest.
## Opening and operating a savings account

Collect and fill the account-opening form (name, address, occupation, specimen signature, photographs); give KYC (Know Your Customer) documents and the introduction of an existing account holder; deposit the minimum amount with a pay-in-slip; the bank issues a passbook and cheque book (and ATM-cum-debit card). The pay-in-slip has two parts: the right-hand foil kept by the bank and the left-hand counterfoil returned to the depositor with the bank's stamp. A cheque deposited is attached to the pay-in-slip. Before paying a cheque the bank checks the signature against the specimen signature. The bank updates the passbook. For a bank, deposits are a liability.

ATM (Automated Teller Machine) — withdraw or deposit cash, check balance any time, 24 × 7. Debit card — pays for purchases directly from one's own bank account. Credit card — buy now on credit up to a limit and pay later, interest charged if not paid in the credit period. Net banking — view balances, transfer funds, open FDs and pay bills over the Internet. Mobile and phone banking, NEFT/RTGS/IMPS transfers, UPI (Unified Payments Interface — fund transfers and bill payments from a mobile), AEPS (Aadhaar Enabled Payment System — transactions with Aadhaar number and fingerprint or iris), and CBS (Core Banking Solution — any-branch banking). An illiterate person can also be given a debit card.

vsa: Mr. Ravi has a limited income and wants to save for future needs. Which account should he open? Why?
A savings bank account — it can be opened with a small amount, money can be deposited any time, it earns interest and can be withdrawn when needed.
Mahesh's father wants to save ₹2,00,000 to gift Mahesh on his graduation day. Which deposit should he open?
A fixed deposit account — a lump sum is deposited for a fixed period and earns a higher rate of interest.
State any two differences between a bank and a moneylender.

(1) Regulation: a bank is regulated by the RBI; a moneylender is not.
(2) Interest: a bank's rate is governed by the RBI and reasonable; a moneylender's is decided by himself and usually very high.
(Also: banks accept deposits; recovery by banks is lawful and flexible.)
Explain the working of net banking.

With net banking the customer logs on to the bank's website with a user ID and password and can, at any time, check the balance and statement, transfer funds, open a fixed deposit, and pay electricity, telephone and other bills without visiting the branch.
What is the difference between a debit card and a credit card?

A debit card pays from the holder's own bank balance, which is reduced at once. A credit card lets the holder buy on credit up to a limit and pay the bank later; interest is charged if not paid within the credit period.
sa: What is e-banking? Explain any two types of e-banking services.

E-banking means doing banking transactions electronically through computers, mobile phones and cards without visiting the branch.
(1) ATM — withdraw cash, check balance, deposit money 24 hours a day.
(2) Net banking — transfer funds, pay bills and open deposits over the Internet.
(Also: debit and credit cards, mobile banking, UPI.)

What is an ATM? How does it help bank customers?

An Automated Teller Machine is an electronic machine installed by banks at convenient places.
It helps customers: (1) withdraw cash at any time, 24 × 7; (2) check balance and get a mini statement; (3) deposit cash and transfer funds without going to the branch.

Explain debit card and credit card.

Debit card: issued to a savings or current account holder; payments made with it are deducted at once from his own balance.
Credit card: lets the holder buy goods on credit up to a fixed limit; the bank pays the seller and the holder repays within the credit period, after which interest is charged. It may be issued to persons with or without an account.

Modes of payment: cash, cheque, demand draft, debit and credit cards, net banking and UPI transfers.

Withdrawals: savings — limited in number; current — any number.

la: Banks provide funds for business and play a vital role in the development of a nation. Explain the role of banking.

(1) Mobilising savings — banks collect the small savings of people and make them available for productive use.
(2) Finance for trade and industry — loans, cash credit and overdrafts help firms buy raw materials and machines.
(3) Help to agriculture and small industries through NABARD, SIDBI and priority-sector lending.
(4) Easy and safe payments — cheques, drafts, cards, net banking and UPI reduce the use of cash.
(5) Balanced regional development — branches in rural and backward areas, credit to weaker sections, promotion of exports.
Commercial banks play a vital role in economic development through primary and secondary functions. Explain any five functions.

(1) Accepting deposits — savings, current, fixed and recurring.
(2) Granting loans and advances — loans, cash credit, overdraft, discounting of bills.
(3) Agency functions — collecting cheques, dividends and interest; paying bills and premiums; buying and selling securities.
(4) General utility functions — demand drafts, traveller's cheques, lockers and safe custody.
(5) Letters of credit, foreign exchange and e-banking services.

HDFC Bank offers many accounts. Geeta, a businesswoman, chose an account with the most liquid deposits and no limit on the number of transactions; her mother opened one for her savings with cheque facility; her brother Kartik deposits ₹3,000 every month for two years. (a) Identify the accounts. (b) Explain two other types of account.

(a) Geeta — current deposit account; her mother — savings bank account; Kartik — recurring deposit account.
(b) Fixed deposit account — a lump sum kept for a fixed period at a higher interest rate.
Multiple option (flexi) deposit — a savings account where amounts above a limit move automatically to a fixed deposit and earn more interest.

or: Anil learns of an account at SBI in which amounts above a limit are transferred automatically to a fixed deposit, combining the benefits of savings and FD. Identify and explain it.

Multiple option deposit account (flexi or sweep account). It works like a savings account for deposits and withdrawals, but when the balance exceeds a set limit the excess is automatically moved into a fixed deposit, earning the higher FD interest; when needed, money comes back from the FD to the savings account. So the customer gets both liquidity and higher interest.

la: Describe the procedure of opening a savings bank account.

(1) Find out the minimum initial deposit and ask for the account-opening form.
(2) Fill the form — name, address, occupation, nominee — and sign; attach photographs.
(3) Give KYC documents (proof of identity and address) and get the introduction of an existing account holder.
(4) Give the specimen signature.
(5) Deposit the initial amount with a pay-in-slip.
(6) The bank opens the account and issues a passbook, cheque book and ATM/debit card.
